source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Headline claim holds inside the paper: a FOK/JOL control layer on fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 lifts pooled accuracy 48.3 to 56.9.
numbers: Pooled N=1,859 (HLE-Verified 668, LiveCodeBench v6 388, R-Bench-V 803). Pass@1 48.3, harness 56.9, +8.6. Avg 2.4 attempts per question.
limits: Single group, single base model, no independent replication found (search 2026-10-25). Code and prompts not yet released at time of paper. Authors' own evaluation.
agent_relevance: Our S0/S6 idea is plausible, but treat as single-source [S]. Must be re-run on our suites.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Compute is NOT equal to plain pass@1. The harness costs about 2.7x the single pass. It beats other multi-sample methods per dollar.
numbers: Cost per question, pooled: pass@1 $0.29; Self-Refine $0.45 (52.4); Budget Forcing $0.67 (51.5); Verifier rerank $1.32 (49.8, 4 attempts); Aggregator $1.42 (53.7, 4 attempts); Harness $0.78 (56.9, 2.4 attempts).
limits: Paper says budgets are matched or closely controlled whenever possible, yet cost and attempts differ across rows. No best-of-2.4 plus vote baseline at the same average spend. Self-Refine on HLE costs $0.41 vs pass@1 $0.50, which looks inconsistent.
agent_relevance: G7 test: compare against the plain model given the same average tokens (about 2.4 samples plus vote). The paper does not do this.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Gains are very uneven by benchmark. Strong on hard code and HLE; none on easy code; modest on multimodal.
numbers: HLE 48.0 to 60.0 (+12.0). LCB 74.3 to 84.3 (+10.0): easy -0.7, medium +1.1, hard +19.6 (vs the listed leaderboard). R-Bench-V 36.1 to 41.1 (+5.0).
limits: Easy LCB is at ceiling (94.7). Leaderboard comparison mixes single-model entries with a multi-attempt system, so beating the leaderboard is not like-for-like.
agent_relevance: Matches G12: spend where there is a foothold. Do not expect gains on easy items.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Ablation on N=100 shows each part helps, but the confidence intervals overlap heavily. Directed retry beats random retry by only 1.3 points at matched K.
numbers: N=100, pass@1 44.0, oracle@4 53.0. Full harness 47.0 [37,57], K=2.58. JOL-only 45.0; FOK-only 42.0; hand rule (1-JOL)*FOK 42.0; random retry matched K 45.7 [43,48]; last-answer 40.0; max-JOL 44.0; no prior metacognitive state 45.0; full prior reasoning context 40.0.
limits: N=100 with 95% bootstrap CIs about +/-10 points. The key claim (directed beats random) rests on 47.0 vs 45.7, not significant. Ablation set is a random subset of the test benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Most of the +8.6 may be extra sampling plus aggregation, in line with G9/G4. Test random retry at matched K at full scale before adopting.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Confidence helps allocate effort across problems, but gives no help choosing among attempts within a problem. This supports our code-selects rule.
numbers: Within-problem JOL std median 0.048; across-problem std 0.270 (5.6x wider). Max-JOL aggregation 44.0 vs pass@1 44.0 (no gain).
quote: JOL scores across attempts often have low variance and do not reliably identify the best candidate answer
limits: Ablation N=100. JOL is a model self-report.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: never select answers by stated confidence. Use confidence only to decide whether to spend more.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Gains sit where the model is unsure. On confident items the harness slightly hurts.
numbers: Accuracy by first-attempt JOL band, pass@1 to harness: low 0.16 to 0.42; medium 0.36 to 0.55; high 0.67 to 0.64 (a drop).
limits: N per band not given in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A trust gate (stop when confident) is right; do not let retry or aggregation override a confident answer. Matches G1.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Harnessable metacognition is rare: only 1 of 9 models passed every diagnosis row. Verbalized confidence is often discriminative but miscalibrated.
numbers: Anchor set N=100. Sonnet-4.6 passes all six rows (FOK, JOL, joint SVM x AUROC, ECE). Opus-4.6 adequate. Six others discriminative but miscalibrated. Gemma-4 fails FOK discrimination. GPT-OSS: JOL AUROC 0.87 but ECE 0.41; SVM brings joint ECE to 0.06.
limits: Anchor set is small and fitted per model; robustness under distribution shift untested (authors say so). Best SVM kernel differs by model (poly, linear, sigmoid, RBF).
agent_relevance: Do not assume stated confidence is usable: run a diagnosis (AUROC, ECE) on our logs first, per model and per problem class. Calibrate in code.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Authors list real limits: model-specific, small anchor set, benchmarks only, no agent tasks.
numbers: DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Gemini-3-Flash named as untested. Agent benchmarks left to future work.
limits: These are the authors' own words (Appendix H).
agent_relevance: Do not generalise to long-horizon agent loops without a test.

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Pre-solve FOK is the weaker signal. Removing FOK costs 2 points and removing JOL costs 5 in the small ablation. The FOK prompt forbids computing first.
numbers: w/o FOK 45.0 vs 47.0; w/o JOL 42.0 vs 47.0 (N=100, CIs about +/-10).
limits: Both inside CI noise. FOK is a self-report made without reasoning.
agent_relevance: A cheap S0 gate could use FOK; test its marginal value on our classes before adding an extra call (G7).

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
finding: Retry design: the next attempt sees prior answers and the model's stated doubts, not prior reasoning. Full-trace context hurt.
numbers: Full previous reasoning context 40.0 vs compact metacognitive history 47.0; no history (independent) 45.0.
limits: N=100; 7-point difference inside overlapping CIs. The anchoring mechanism is argued, not isolated.
agent_relevance: Fits the G2/G10 spirit: pass feedback, not the failed text. Our S5 REVISE should test critique-only vs full trace at equal tokens.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Intrinsic self-correction (no oracle) lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after 2 rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA 59.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and changes correct to wrong more often than wrong to right.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: 2023-era models; short-answer tasks; generic self-correction prompts. Later reasoning models may differ.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: no revision from the model's own opinion. The Cao harness avoids asking the model to critique its trace, but still relies on self-reported JOL.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal numbers of responses. Some self-correction gains came from weak first prompts.
numbers: GSM8K gpt-3.5: debate (3 agents, 2 rounds, 9 responses) 83.0 vs self-consistency with 9 responses 88.2; single response 76.7; SC 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3. Folding the feedback instructions into the first prompt beat self-correction.
limits: Same model-era limits. One model, one dataset for debate.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 and the equal-compute standard we apply to the harness: always compare to SC at the same response count.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Critical survey: no prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback on general tasks. It works when reliable external feedback exists, or after large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Three findings: (1) no reliable evidence of prompted self-correction in general tasks; (2) works with reliable external feedback (code interpreters, search, tools); (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Gives an experiment-design checklist.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey covers work to May 2024. Some tasks are exceptionally suited (decomposable, easy to verify). Reasoning-model era only briefly covered. I read the abstract and introduction text, not the full survey.
agent_relevance: The harness retry uses self-JOL, not external checks. Our G2/G3 (revise from real output, pass on held-out check) is the stricter design.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL 2024)
finding: Models fail at finding logical mistakes in chain of thought, but correct well when told where the mistake is. The bottleneck is mistake finding.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 CoT traces, 5 tasks. Best model GPT-4 reaches only 52.87 overall accuracy on direct step-level mistake finding. Backtracking with the oracle mistake location raises downstream accuracy. Net change depends on base accuracy (the paper's own example: 50% start gives 68.6, 99% start gives 92.8).
quote: poor self-correction performance stems from LLMs' inability to find logical mistakes
limits: Needs oracle location; a small trained classifier is proposed (about 60-70% accuracy). Dataset skewed toward incorrect traces. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Fits G2: locate the failure with code (test output), then ask the model to fix it. Do not ask the model to find its own error.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs (ICLR 2024)
finding: Verbalized confidence is overconfident and a poor failure predictor. Agreement across samples is much better. The gap to white-box methods is small.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 8 datasets. GPT-4 vanilla verbalized confidence: average AUROC 62.7 (random is 50). GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. Sampling 5 responses with consistency raised GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7%. White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522 (abstract). AUROC about 22.2% better from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
quote: LLMs tend to be highly overconfident when verbalizing
limits: 2023-era models. No method is best everywhere; all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks. Gains saturate by M of about 5 to 13 samples.
agent_relevance: Rival view to Cao: one self-report is weak, agreement across 3-5 short samples is strong. Supports logging consistency (SUBFIELDS dig-into 1). Tension with G4: agreement is a hint, not proof.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions when the format is right. P(True) self-evaluation works, better when the model sees many of its own samples. A trained P(IK) head partly transfers.
numbers: Calibration improves with scale (up to 52B). P(IK) trained on TriviaQA alone generalises partly to other tasks; training on all tasks improves AUROC on all (Table 1). Few-shot self-evaluation is calibrated, zero-shot is not; larger k mainly improves calibration, not AUROC. A None-of-the-above option harms performance and calibration.
limits: Needs a trained head or logprobs, not available in a black-box scaffold; poor calibration on new tasks. RLHF policies are miscalibrated until temperature tuned. I did not extract per-task AUROC values.
agent_relevance: Prompted self-report (as in Cao) is the weaker cousin; Cao's SVM calibration head is the fix. Few-shot format matters.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and voting beats greedy CoT. The agreement rate predicts correctness, so it doubles as an uncertainty signal.
numbers: PaLM-540B, 40 paths, 10-run averages: GSM8K 56.5 to 74.4 (+17.9); SVAMP 79.0 to 86.6; AQuA 35.8 to 48.3; StrategyQA 75.3 to 81.6; ARC-c 85.2 to 88.7. Most gain comes in the first 5 to 10 paths.
quote: consistency ... is highly correlated with accuracy
limits: Compute grows linearly with paths. Gains shrink as models get stronger. Errors are correlated, so voting has a ceiling.
agent_relevance: The baseline any know-when-to-retry harness must beat at equal samples. A natural stop rule: stop when k short samples agree.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Stopping sampling once a window of answers agrees saves most samples at almost no accuracy cost on easy tasks.
numbers: Sample reduction vs SC: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. GPT-4 accuracy change 0.00 on MATH, GSM8K, CSQA; -0.02 Last Letters. Weaker models lose more: GPT-3.5 StrategyQA -0.19; Llama-2 7B StrategyQA -0.14, Coin Flip -0.14. Window 5 (8 on MATH), max 40 (64) samples, 10 runs.
quote: ESC significantly reduces costs while barely affecting performance
limits: Accuracy loss grows with weaker models; small saving on hard tasks (Llama-2 MATH saved 1.52 of 64 samples). Agreement is not proof (G4).
agent_relevance: A code-only stop rule (window agreement) competes with model-rated JOL at no extra calls. Test head-to-head at equal tokens.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Using the model's own token-level confidence to filter or stop traces improves accuracy and cuts tokens versus majority voting, but fails when the model is confidently wrong.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 at 512 traces: DeepConf 99.9% vs majority vote 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8%. Online mode cuts tokens up to 84.7% (97.9% accuracy with DeepConf-low). DeepSeek-8B AIME25 82.3 to 87.4 offline; Qwen3-32B AIME24 85.3 to 90.8. Top-10% filtering helps in 12 of 20 offline settings (average +1.22 points) and hurts in 8 of 20 by up to 4.69 points.
quote: rare cases where confidence concentrates on an incorrect answer
limits: Needs token logprobs (white-box). Confident-wrong traces break it; GPT-OSS-120B on HMMT25 hurt by aggressive filtering. 16-trace warm-up. Read via fetch summary of the HTML (first 100k of 107k characters).
agent_relevance: A white-box signal beats voting in most but not all settings; failures come from overconfidence. Use signals for stopping with a conservative fallback.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Allocating test-time compute by question difficulty is about 4x more efficient than uniform best-of-N. Which method helps depends on difficulty. The hardest questions gain little from any method.
numbers: Revisions beat best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (64 vs 256 samples); PRM search 16 vs 64 generations. Easy questions: sequential revisions best, beam search degrades with budget; medium-hard: beam search beats best-of-N; level 5: no method makes much progress. Against a roughly 14x larger model at matched FLOPs, test-time compute wins on easy and medium questions or low inference load; pretraining wins on the hardest.
limits: Difficulty needs an oracle (2048 samples) or a learned verifier score; the cost of estimating it is not counted. MATH and PaLM-2 only. Read via fetch summary of the first 100k of 111k characters.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for G12 and for the Cao idea of adaptive allocation. A cheap difficulty predictor is the crux.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models burn tokens on easy questions with little accuracy gain. Self-training on shorter outputs halves tokens at kept accuracy.
numbers: For 2 plus 3, o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models (13 solutions in one example). Self-training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview at kept accuracy. 2-4 solution rounds in 76-80% of QwQ cases; more rounds on easier test sets.
limits: Training-based fix, not a scaffold. Late-2024 to early-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and the Cao observation (Fig 1c) that unharnessed models do not allocate effort by confidence. A code-side early stop could recover this without training.

source: Jeong et al. (2024) Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented LLMs through Question Complexity
finding: A small classifier that routes queries to no retrieval, single-step or multi-step retrieval matches multi-step quality at under half the time. The router is only about 55% accurate.
numbers: GPT-3.5, 6 datasets x 500 queries. No retrieval F1 48.56/Acc 44.27; single-step 46.99/45.27; Mallen adaptive retrieval 48.20/45.30 (0.50 steps); multi-step IRCoT 50.87/49.70 at 3.33x time; Adaptive-RAG 50.91/48.97 at 1.46x time; oracle router 62.80/58.57. Classifier accuracy 54.52% (No 30.52, One 66.28, Multi 65.45).
limits: One run per setting; auto-labelled training data; only 3 complexity levels; large gap to the oracle router. Self-RAG row used a different base model.
agent_relevance: Uncertainty-triggered retrieval works but router quality is the limit. The oracle gap (+11.9 F1) shows the headroom. Always-on single-step retrieval is worse than none on F1.

source: Wen et al. (2024) Know Your Limits: A Survey of Abstention in Large Language Models
finding: Abstention triggers span query, model-knowledge and human-values views. Common failures are over-abstention and overconfident verbal uncertainty. No single metric captures quality.
numbers: No pooled effect size. Sub-findings: verbalized confidence is overconfident; finetuning on unfamiliar examples can raise hallucination (Gekhman et al.); first-person hedges lowered user trust (Kim et al. 2024b). Metrics: abstain accuracy, ARSP (over-abstention), coverage, AURCC.
limits: Survey; mostly qualitative. I read the first 100k of 136k characters of the page text.
agent_relevance: Matches G6: abstaining has a cost. Score coverage and accuracy together, and count over-abstention.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Appending Wait to extend thinking helps a little and then flattens. Sequential extension alone is limited; parallel methods scale further.
numbers: s1-32B on AIME24: 50.0 without extension, 53.3 with 2x Wait, up to 57% at the best budget-forcing setting. Extension flattens out at about six times. Too much suppression causes loops. REBASE tree search scaled better than majority voting and than sequential scaling.
limits: Fine-tuned model; AIME24 has 30 questions, so one question is 3.3 points. Used by Cao et al. as the vertical baseline ($0.67, 51.5).
agent_relevance: Forcing more thinking is blind, not a monitor. In Cao's table it is beaten on cost and accuracy, consistent with G11.

source: Cao et al. (2026) metacognitive harness, Appendix F per-benchmark cost tables
finding: On R-Bench-V the harness costs 4.8x pass@1 and verifier reranking loses accuracy.
numbers: R-Bench-V: pass@1 36.1 at $0.15; harness 41.1 at $0.72, K=3.2; Self-Refine 38.2 at $0.55; budget forcing 38.2 at $0.80; verifier rerank 34.0 (-2.1) at $0.80; aggregator 36.5 at $0.90. LCB: pass@1 74.3 at $0.24; harness 84.3 at $0.56, K=2.6; aggregator 83.4 at $0.94 (K=4). HLE: pass@1 48.0 at $0.50; harness 60.0 at $0.98, K=1.4; aggregator 57.0 at $2.31.
limits: Cost is total inference cost divided by questions; token counts not shown. One run per condition.
agent_relevance: Gain per extra dollar differs by task: strong on HLE (+12.0 for +$0.48), weaker on RBV (+5.0 for +$0.57). A prior for class-dependent gating.

source: Cao et al. (2026) metacognitive harness, Fig 1 and Appendix A (unharnessed behaviour)
finding: Without a harness, models report confidence that predicts correctness but do not spend more effort on low-confidence items.
numbers: Nine LLMs evaluated. Higher FOK/JOL bands have higher accuracy; reasoning length does not reliably rise for low-confidence bands (Fig 1c). After harnessing, attempts fall monotonically from low to high confidence for both FOK and JOL.
limits: Reasoning length is a coarse effort proxy. Per-model arrow counts are in a figure I read only as text.
agent_relevance: Matches the know-but-do-not-act framing and our G1 rule: act on a code-checked gate, not on the model's own urge.

source: Cao et al. (2026) metacognitive harness, pipeline details relevant to our schema
finding: The harness copies the selected attempt verbatim, and the aggregator is a model that sees reasoning and answers but not confidence scores.
numbers: Pipeline: FOK once, then Solve plus JOL in one call, up to K=4, SVM stop rule p_stop=0.7 on (FOK, JOL), then a forced aggregator picks an attempt index. Case G.2: low FOK overridden by high JOL, stops at K=1.
limits: The aggregator is still a model judge, so the G5 bias warning (length, authorship) applies; the authors do not test judge bias. SVM calibrated on N=100 anchors.
agent_relevance: Our version should replace the model aggregator with code checks where a check exists, and keep a model judge only for ungradeable items.
